newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian business pins hopes on budget tax changes.
newsitem.headline: Indian business pins hopes on budget tax changes.

text.p: Indian industry, grappling with high interest rates and flagging output growth, expects the government to remove some painful corporate taxes in the federal budget, top business leaders said on Thursday.

They said the 1997/98 budget for the fiscal year starting on April 1 would need to scrap a controversial tax on profits and a surcharge on corporate tax to revive languid capital markets and spur industrial growth.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram was set to present the budget to parliament at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT) on Friday.

Hira Lall Somany, president of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India, said the 12.9 percent minimum alternate tax (MAT) on profits introduced last July had seriously hurt business.
"MAT must be removed because it has already done very major damage," Somany told Reuters in an interview.
"But the government's cheapest methods to help growth are to remove double taxation of dividends and remove the surcharge on corporate tax."
India levies a 40 percent tax on corporate profits and a further surcharge of 7.5 percent. The government also taxes shareholders on dividends, which are paid out of taxed profits.

Confederation of Indian Industry president Shekhar Datta said high interest rates were reining in output growth rather than rising inflation. Indian banks' annual prime lending rates range between 14.5 percent and 18.5 percent.

"Interest rates are the prime reason for the industrial slowdown. But they can be brought down only if the fiscal deficit is brought down first. Industry is somewhat crowded out of the capital markets by the government," he told Reuters.
India has targeted the fiscal deficit, comprising the budget deficit and government borrowings, at 5.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97 against 5.9 percent in 1995/96.
The government says it is committed to trimming the deficit to four percent of GDP as quickly as possible.

"The fundamentals of the Indian economy are still strong, although there has been a slowdown in exports and industrial growth," said Amit Mitra, secretary-general of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
"But if the budget is uninspiring, then we may begin to see the vitals being affected. This budget will be a cutting-edge budget for India. Either the nation wins or the confidence level drops."
India's exports are estimated to grow by eight to 10 percent in 1996/97 over the previous fiscal year. That would compare with 18-21 percent growth during the three preceding years.
The government has forecast 1996/97 industrial growth at about 10 percent, compared to 11.7 percent in 1995/96.
Datta said Indian businesses were going through a process of consolidating and focusing on their core strengths -- a phase which had also slowed output growth.
But the benefits of such consolidation were being swallowed by a tax on capital gains due to corporate restructuring, which the government must remove, Somany said.
India should also press ahead with making the rupee convertible on the capital account, both Somany and Datta said.
The rupee can currently be converted freely for transactions in goods and services but the government exercises control over capital transactions.
